analysis.one_liner: Gives workers at larger companies twelve weeks of unpaid family and medical leave and expands federal child and family programs.
analysis.headline: The bill, including a family-leave right Congress had already passed once, sat in four House committees without a hearing or vote and died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This omnibus bill would have entitled employees at employers with 50 or more workers to twelve weeks of unpaid leave for a birth, adoption, family medical emergency, or their own serious illness, with their job and health coverage protected. It also would have shielded Head Start, WIC, and child immunization funding from annual spending caps, created a home-visit parent-education program, turned family preservation services into a federal entitlement that grew from $200 million toward $600 million a year, and tightened rules for foster care and adoption. The bill never received a hearing, committee vote, or floor vote in any chamber.
analysis.who_benefits: Working people: employees who need time for a birth, adoption, or serious illness without losing their job or health coverage; low-income families served by Head Start, WIC, and immunization programs, which would be protected from budget caps; parents of young children who would get home visiting and developmental screening; and children in foster care, whose cases would face faster reviews and whose states would get guaranteed family preservation funding.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Parents, seriously ill workers, and foster children

how_it_helps.text: Title I entitles employees with at least 12 months and 1,250 hours of service to 12 workweeks of unpaid leave for the birth or adoption of a child, to care for a seriously ill spouse, child, or parent, or for their own serious health condition, and requires restoration to the same or an equivalent job and continued health coverage during leave.
Employers may not interfere with or fire workers for taking leave or for filing complaints, and the Labor Department and courts can enforce the right with damages and attorney's fees.

Title II treats the costs of Head Start, child immunization grants, and the WIC nutrition program as emergency funding exempt from the annual discretionary spending caps for fiscal years 1992 through 1995.

Title IV creates a mandatory family preservation entitlement starting at $200 million in fiscal 1993 and rising to $600 million by fiscal 1997, aimed at keeping families in crisis together and reducing foster care placements, and shortens the deadline for deciding a foster child's permanent status from 18 months to 12.

Title III authorizes $20 million a year for 'Parents as Teachers' grants for home visits and developmental screening for families from pregnancy through age three, prioritizing teen, low-income, and other hard-to-serve parents.
The bill applies the same leave rights to congressional employees, covering the House and Senate workforce alongside private-sector workers.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 50 or more employees, who would have to hold jobs open, maintain health coverage for workers on unpaid leave, and face damages and fees if they interfered with leave; and federal taxpayers, who would fund the new family preservation entitlement and the Parents as Teachers grants.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers with 50+ workers and federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The leave is unpaid, so a worker who needs twelve weeks off can lose a full quarter's income unless the employer or worker can substitute accrued paid leave; nothing in the bill requires employers to provide paid leave where they do not already.
Coverage is limited: employers below 50 workers are exempt, and workers with less than 12 months or 1,250 hours with their employer are not eligible, leaving out many part-time and newer employees.

Employers would bear the cost of holding positions open and continuing health premiums during unpaid leave, a cost that falls hardest on mid-sized firms near the 50-employee threshold and that businesses argued could discourage hiring.
Declaring Head Start, WIC, and immunization spending 'emergency' funding exempts it from the discretionary spending caps, weakening the budget discipline those caps were enacted to enforce.

The bill overlaps multiple committees and programs, and small state programs like the Missouri-based Parents as Teachers model get a dedicated federal center and funding preference, which critics could call narrow targeting.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is real and wide: a job-protected right to take time for births and illness, which at the time no federal law guaranteed, plus steady funding for programs serving young and low-income children. The honest costs are that the leave is unpaid, which limits its value to the lowest-paid workers it most aims to help, that smaller firms are carved out, and that removing three popular programs from the budget caps weakens spending discipline. The design is a compromise—the leave is unpaid and modest in scope—but it is not badly built for its purpose.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in September 1992, referred to four House committees and then to subcommittees in each, never got a hearing or vote anywhere, and expired when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Patricia Schroeder introduced the Family Investment Act of 1992 in the House on September 17, 1992.
Sixteen representatives cosponsored the bill, fourteen Democrats and two Republicans.
The same day it was referred to four committees: Education and Labor, House Administration, Post Office and Civil Service, and Ways and Means.

Over the following three weeks it was referred to subcommittees in all four committees, including Human Resources, Personnel and Police, Compensation and Employee Benefits, and Labor-Management Relations.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded; the bill never advanced after the subcommittee referrals and died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

Its leave title was essentially the same Family and Medical Leave bill that had passed both chambers of Congress in 1991, been vetoed by President George H.W. Bush, and failed to overcome the veto in the Senate by a single vote in early 1992.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have had to provide the leave mandate came out ahead, along with strict budget-cap supporters who avoided exempting three large programs from the spending limits. Workers had to wait until the next Congress, when a similar family leave bill passed and was signed in 1993.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers spared the leave mandate and capkeepers

for.name: Rep. Patricia Schroeder
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled the family leave, child welfare, and early-childhood titles into one package.

for.name: 16 House cosponsors (14 Democrats, 2 Republicans)
for.role: Original cosponsors, including Reps. Wheat, Gilman, Green of New York, Lehman, Martinez, Collins of Michigan, and Downey

against.name: Rep. William D. Ford
against.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Committee received the referral and never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill.

against.name: Rep. Dan Rostenkowski
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill's spending titles never acted on it.

against.name: President George H.W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Had vetoed the same family and medical leave bill passed by Congress in 1991 and opposed requiring employers to provide such leave, signaling any similar bill faced a veto.

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly all Democratic (14 of 16 cosponsors) with two Republican exceptions, and the 1991 veto fight over the identical leave proposal had split by party; the bill itself never reached a roll-call vote.

industries.note: They would have had to hold jobs open for up to twelve weeks, keep paying health premiums during unpaid leave, and face damages and attorney's fees for violations. Exemptions for firms under 50 workers concentrated the cost on larger and mid-sized employers.
The bill requires group health coverage to be maintained at the employer's expense while a worker is on leave, keeping premiums flowing during the leave period.

industries.industry: Head Start, WIC, and immunization service providers
industries.note: Their federal funding would be treated as emergency spending outside the annual discretionary caps, protecting it from cuts, with more predictable support for low-income families.

industries.industry: State and private child welfare and family preservation agencies
industries.note: A new entitlement starting at $200 million a year would fund services to keep families together and improve foster care and adoption systems.
